headline: Burnham uses first conference speech as PM to promise a 'new social contract' and voting reform

terms.meaning: An unwritten deal about what citizens give the state and what the state provides in return.
A voting system where seats in Parliament roughly match each party's share of the vote.
Limits a government sets on how much it can borrow and spend.

levels.headline: Burnham uses first conference speech as PM to promise a 'new social contract' and voting reform
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as party leader, delivered in Liverpool on 29 September 2026, to promise a 'new social contract for the 21st century' and a large expansion of public services.
He proposed a state pension that rises every year, an end to care charges and a National Care Service that would be free at the point of use and paid for through taxation, in principle like the NHS. He also pledged that low-income pensioners would not be pulled into paying income tax during this Parliament.
Burnham said Labour would fight the next general election on a promise to replace the winner-takes-all system with a form of proportional representation, though the details have not been set. He also promised a reset of relations with European neighbours.
He accepted there would be costs and trade-offs. He warned that difficult decisions on welfare and pension spending would be needed, said the government would stick to its fiscal rules to bring borrowing and debt down, and acknowledged that some plans would take longer than one Parliament to deliver.
Burnham became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, after Keir Starmer stood down. The speech was his main chance to set out how his government differs from its predecessor, while the Budget on 28 October will show how much of it can be paid for.
levels.why: It shows the new Prime Minister's priorities, and how far they can be funded within strict borrowing limits.

levels.headline: Burnham pledges a 'new social contract' and electoral reform at Labour conference
levels.body:
Andy Burnham, who became Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, used his first Labour conference speech as leader on 29 September in Liverpool to promise a 'new social contract for the 21st century'.
His headline offers were for older people and carers: a state pension that rises every year, an end to care charges, and a National Care Service free at the point of use and funded from general taxation. He said low-income pensioners would not be dragged into paying income tax in this Parliament.
He also said Labour would go into the next election promising to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation, without saying which form. A reset of ties with Europe was part of the package too.
Burnham was open about the price. Some welfare and pension spending decisions would be hard, the government would keep to its fiscal rules on borrowing and debt, and some reforms would take more than one Parliament.
The speech sets expectations ahead of the Budget on 28 October, when the Chancellor must show how the promises are paid for.
levels.why: It sets the political agenda for the new government and raises questions about how it will be paid for.

levels.headline: Burnham promises a new deal on care and pensions, and a fairer voting system
levels.body:
In his first conference speech as Labour leader and Prime Minister, delivered in Liverpool on 29 September, Andy Burnham promised a 'new social contract' between the state and the public.
The main ideas were a state pension that goes up every year, no more care charges, and a National Care Service that would be free when people use it and paid for by taxes, much like the NHS. Low-income pensioners would not have to pay income tax during this Parliament.
He also said Labour would fight the next election on changing how MPs are elected, moving to a form of proportional representation, where a party's share of seats is closer to its share of votes. He promised closer ties with Europe as well.
Burnham admitted that this would cost money and some choices would be difficult, including on welfare and pensions. He said the government would still obey its fiscal rules, which limit borrowing, and that some changes would take longer than one Parliament.
He took over as Prime Minister on 20 July 2026, so this was his chance to explain his plans to the party.
levels.why: It tells voters what the new Prime Minister wants to do and how he plans to pay for it.

levels.headline: Burnham sets out his plans for care, pensions and elections
levels.body:
Andy Burnham gave his first speech to the Labour conference as Prime Minister in Liverpool on 29 September. He called his plan a 'new social contract'. That means a fresh understanding of what people put in and what the state gives back.
He said the state pension would rise every year, care charges would end and a National Care Service would be set up. It would be free to use and paid for through taxes. He also said that poorer pensioners would not pay income tax in this Parliament.
He said Labour would ask voters at the next election to back proportional representation. Under this system the number of seats a party wins matches its share of the vote more closely than it does now. He also wants better relations with Europe.
Burnham said the plans have a cost. Some decisions on welfare and pensions will be hard, and the government will stay within its rules on borrowing. He added that some changes will take longer than one Parliament.
He has been Prime Minister since 20 July 2026, after Keir Starmer stepped down.
levels.why: It shows what the government wants to change, and why people will watch to see if it can afford it.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister promises more help with care and pensions, and a change to voting
levels.body:
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, made a big speech to his party in Liverpool on 29 September. It was his first conference speech as leader. He talked about a 'new social contract', which means a fresh deal between the government and the public about who gives what and who gets what.
He made several promises. The state pension would go up every year. People would stop paying charges for care. There would be a National Care Service, free to use and paid for out of taxes, a bit like the NHS. Pensioners on low incomes would not have to pay income tax while this Parliament lasts.
He also said Labour would fight the next election on changing the voting system. The new system would be a form of proportional representation, which gives each party seats in line with its share of votes.
Burnham said it would not be easy. Some choices on benefits and pensions would be hard, and the government would stick to its rules on borrowing. Some of the changes would take years.
levels.why: It affects older people, carers and voters, and shows how the government plans to spend.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister has made big promises about care, pensions and voting
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. He has led the country since 20 July 2026. On 29 September he gave a big speech to his party, Labour, in the city of Liverpool.
He said he wants a 'new social contract'. This is a way of saying a new deal between the people and the government. He promised that the state pension, the money older people get from the government, would go up every year. He said people would no longer pay charges for care. Care means help with things like washing and dressing for people who cannot manage alone. He wants a National Care Service that is free to use and paid for by taxes. Poorer pensioners would not pay income tax.
He also wants to change how people vote. Today, whoever wins the most votes in an area wins the seat. Burnham wants a system called proportional representation, where parties get seats in line with the votes they get.
He said some of this will be hard to pay for, and it will take time.
levels.why: It could change how older people are looked after and how elections work.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister wants to change how care, pensions and voting work
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. On 29 September he made a long speech to the Labour Party in Liverpool. He wants the government to make a new deal with the public.
He made some promises. Older people would get a bigger state pension every year. The state pension is money the government pays to people who are older. People would not have to pay charges for care. Care is help for people who cannot look after themselves. The government would start a new service for care, and it would be free to use. Taxes would pay for it. Taxes are the money we all pay to the government. Some pensioners with small incomes would not pay income tax.
He also said he would like to change how MPs are chosen. MPs are the people we vote for to run the country. At the moment, one person wins in each area. He wants a fairer way, where each party gets seats to match its votes.
He said it will cost money, and some jobs will take a long time.
levels.why: It shows what the person running the country plans to do next.

levels.headline: The Prime Minister has a plan to change how we look after older people
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister, which means he is the person in charge of the government. On 29 September he gave a big speech to his party, Labour, in a city called Liverpool.
He said he wants a 'new social contract'. That just means a new deal between the government and everyone else. He promised that the state pension would go up every year. The state pension is money the government pays to older people. He also said people should stop paying charges for care, which is help for people who cannot manage everyday jobs by themselves. A new National Care Service would be free to use, and taxes would pay for it. Taxes are the money people pay to the government.
He said he wants to change how MPs are chosen, so that each party gets a fair number of seats for the votes it wins. MPs are the people who work in Parliament to make the rules.
He said it will cost money and take time, so some choices will be hard.
levels.why: It shows the changes the leader of the country wants to make.

levels.headline: The leader of the country has some big plans
levels.body:
Andy Burnham is the Prime Minister. He is the person in charge of the country's government. He gave a big speech on 29 September in a city called Liverpool.
He told people about his plans. He wants older people to get a bit more money from the government each year. This is called the state pension. He wants people who need help looking after someone to stop paying for it. He also wants a new care service. It would help people who cannot look after themselves. It would not cost them anything when they use it. We would all pay for it with our taxes. Taxes are money we give to the government to pay for things like schools and hospitals.
He also wants to change how we choose MPs. MPs are the people who help make the rules. He wants the choosing to be fairer.
He said it will cost a lot. Some plans will take a long time, and some will be hard to do.
levels.why: It tells us what the leader wants to change to help people.

levels.headline: A leader makes a promise to help older people
levels.body:
Imagine your school had a new head teacher. On a big day, she stands up and tells everyone what she plans to do. That is a bit like what happened here. The new leader of the country is called the Prime Minister. His name is Andy Burnham.
He stood up in front of lots of people and said what he wants to do. He wants to help older people. They would get a little more pocket money from the government each year. He also wants to help people who need looking after, like people who are too poorly or too old to cook or get dressed on their own. That help would be free when they need it.
He also wants to change how grown-ups vote, to make it fairer, a bit like making sure everyone gets a fair turn in a playground game.
But he said it will cost lots of money, so it will take time.
levels.why: It is a leader saying how he hopes to make life kinder for older people.

headline: Chancellor John Healey sets 28 October for his first Budget, promising fiscal discipline

terms.meaning: The Chancellor's yearly statement setting out tax and spending plans.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the economy and public finances.
Limits a government sets on how much it can borrow and spend.

levels.headline: Chancellor John Healey sets 28 October for his first Budget, promising fiscal discipline
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026, about three months after the Burnham government took office.
Healey confirmed the date in a video message and, according to reports, in a letter to the Treasury Select Committee on 31 July. He asked the Office for Budget Responsibility to publish its economic and fiscal forecast on the same day.
Healey has said the Budget will be built on fiscal discipline and will meet the government's fiscal rules. He has also described a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode in Britain.
Details of tax and spending changes have not been announced. The Institute for Government says the Chancellor will need to set a clear course for the rest of the Parliament, reassure financial markets, and show a convincing story on growth and on how extra spending would be funded.
The date also falls within a tense economic backdrop, with inflation at 3.1% in August, Bank Rate at 3.75% and the Bank of England's next decision due on 5 November. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised large public service reforms that will have to be paid for.
levels.why: The Budget will decide taxes and spending for millions of people and test whether the government's promises add up.

levels.headline: Healey will deliver his first Budget on 28 October
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, will deliver his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026, roughly three months into the Burnham government.
He announced the date in a video message and reportedly told the Treasury Select Committee in a letter dated 31 July. The independent Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its economic and fiscal forecast on the same day.
Healey says the Budget will be based on fiscal discipline and will meet the government's fiscal rules, which limit borrowing and debt. He has also said it will move money and power away from Westminster to every part of Britain.
No tax or spending decisions have been revealed. The Institute for Government says Healey must set a course for the rest of the Parliament, reassure bond markets and show a credible plan for growth and for funding extra spending.
The Budget comes with inflation at 3.1%, Bank Rate at 3.75%, and new promises from the Prime Minister on care and pensions to be funded.
levels.why: It will show whether the government's spending promises can be paid for within its own rules.

levels.headline: The Chancellor has set the date for his first Budget: 28 October
levels.body:
John Healey, the Chancellor, will present his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026. This is about three months after Andy Burnham's government came into office.
He confirmed the date in a video message. The Office for Budget Responsibility, an independent group that predicts how the economy will do, will publish its forecast on the same day.
Healey says the plan will be based on fiscal discipline and will meet the government's fiscal rules, the limits on how much it can borrow. He also says it will move money and power out of Westminster and spread it around the country.
We do not yet know what will happen to taxes or spending. The Institute for Government, a think tank, says the Chancellor needs to give a clear plan for the rest of the Parliament, reassure investors and explain how he will fund new spending.
Prices are rising by 3.1% a year, and the Prime Minister has promised bigger help for pensioners and carers, so the sums matter.
levels.why: Budget decisions affect taxes, public services and the cost of borrowing for everyone.

levels.headline: Chancellor announces his first Budget will be on 28 October
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, will give his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026. The Budget is the big yearly statement where the government says how it will raise money through taxes and how it will spend it. It comes about three months after the new government under Andy Burnham started work.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, which gives independent forecasts for the economy, will publish its predictions on the same day.
Healey says he will be careful with the public finances and stay within the government's own rules on borrowing. He also wants to move money and power out of London to every part of Britain.
Nothing has been said yet about which taxes might change. The Institute for Government says he needs a clear plan for the next few years, must keep investors calm, and must show how he will grow the economy and pay for new promises.
Prices are rising at 3.1% a year, which makes the choices harder.
levels.why: It will affect what people pay in tax and what the government can afford to do.

levels.headline: The Chancellor will say how the government plans to spend money on 28 October
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the minister in charge of the government's money. His name is John Healey, and he will give his first Budget on Wednesday 28 October 2026. A Budget is a big speech where the Chancellor says how much tax people will pay and what the government will spend it on.
A group called the Office for Budget Responsibility will share its own forecast that day. It is independent, which means the government does not tell it what to say. It tries to guess how the economy will do.
Healey says he will be careful with money and follow the government's rules on borrowing. He also says he wants more money and power to go to places all around the country, not just London.
We do not know yet what will change. Experts say he must have a clear plan, keep people who lend money to the government feeling safe, and say how he will pay for new ideas.
Prices are going up by 3.1% a year, so money is tight.
levels.why: It could change taxes and public services that people use every day.

levels.headline: The person in charge of the country's money has picked a date for his big speech
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the government minister who looks after the country's money. This Chancellor is called John Healey. On Wednesday 28 October 2026 he will give a big speech called the Budget. In it, he explains how much tax people and businesses will pay, and what the government will spend money on, like schools, hospitals and roads.
On the same day, a group called the Office for Budget Responsibility will say how it thinks the economy will go. It is independent, so it does not take orders from the government.
Mr Healey says he will be careful and follow the rules the government has set about borrowing. Borrowing means taking money now and paying it back later. He also wants to share money and power with towns and cities across Britain.
Nobody knows yet what he will say. Some experts say he needs a clear plan and must show how new ideas will be paid for. Prices are rising, so this is not easy.
levels.why: The Budget decides how the government gets and spends money that affects everyone.

levels.headline: A big speech about money is coming on 28 October
levels.body:
The Chancellor looks after the money for the whole country. His name is John Healey. He will make a big speech called the Budget on 28 October. In it he says how the government will get money and how it will spend it.
The government gets most of its money from taxes. Taxes are small amounts that people and businesses pay. The government uses the money for things like schools, hospitals and roads.
A team of experts called the OBR will also say what it thinks will happen to the economy. The economy is all the buying, selling and working that goes on in the country. The OBR is independent, so it can tell the truth even if the government may not like it.
Mr Healey says he will be careful with money. He will not borrow too much. He also wants to share out more money and power to places all over the country.
No one knows what he will say yet. Prices are going up, so it will be tricky.
levels.why: It will decide how much money there is for things we all use.

levels.headline: The Chancellor will explain how the government will get and spend money
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the minister in charge of the government's money. He is called John Healey. On Wednesday 28 October he will give a speech called the Budget. In it he will say how much tax people and businesses must pay, and what the government will spend money on, such as schools, hospitals and roads.
On the same day, a group called the Office for Budget Responsibility will say how it thinks the economy will do. The government does not tell it what to say, which is why people trust it.
Mr Healey says he will be careful and keep to the rules about borrowing. Borrowing means getting money now and paying it back later. He also says he wants more money and power to go to towns and cities around the country, not only London.
No one knows what he will say yet. Prices are rising by 3.1% a year, so the choices will be tricky.
levels.why: The Budget decides taxes and spending that affect families, schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The Chancellor will tell us how the country's money will be used
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person who looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he will give a big talk called the Budget. He will say how the government will collect money and how it will use it.
The government collects money from taxes. Taxes are money that grown-ups give to the government from their wages and when they buy things. The government uses this money to pay for schools, hospitals and roads.
Some clever people called the OBR will say how they think the country's money will go. They do not work for the government, so they can say what they really think.
Mr Healey says he will be careful. He will try not to borrow too much. Borrowing is when you take money and promise to give it back later. He also wants to share more money and power with places all across the country.
We do not know what he will say yet. Things in shops cost more now, so it will not be easy.
levels.why: What he decides will change what the government can pay for.

levels.headline: A big day is coming for the country's money
levels.body:
Think about how your family decides what to spend its money on. Mum or Dad might say, 'We can pay for the holiday but not a new car.' The country does something like this too. The person who decides is called the Chancellor. His name is John Healey.
On 28 October, he will give a big talk called the Budget. He will say how much money the government will collect from taxes, which is money grown-ups pay. He will also say what it will spend the money on, like schools and hospitals.
He says he will be careful, like someone who does not want to spend more than they have. He also wants to share money with towns and cities everywhere, not only the capital.
Nobody knows yet what he will say. Some things in shops cost more than before, so he has to choose carefully.
levels.why: It is like a family deciding what it can afford, but for a whole country.

headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it

terms.meaning: The interest rate set by the Bank of England, which influences mortgage, loan and savings rates.
The Monetary Policy Committee, the nine people who vote on Bank Rate.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75% as three members vote to raise it
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% on 17 September 2026, but the vote was split 6 to 3. Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voted for a quarter-point rise to 4%.
The committee said the risks to inflation are tilted to the upside and that it stands ready to act. It blamed the rise in inflation on the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy prices, and said further increases are expected in coming quarters.
The majority judged that waiting was the better option. UK consumer price inflation reached 3.1% in the year to August, well above the 2% target, with energy and especially motor fuels accounting for much of the overshoot. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.6%.
Bank Rate was last cut in December 2025 to 3.75% and has since been held. The next decision is on 5 November, alongside the November Monetary Policy Report. Markets and mortgage commentators are watching closely for a possible rise, which would push up the cost of variable-rate mortgages and loans.
levels.why: Bank Rate sets the cost of borrowing across the economy, so a move towards a rise matters to borrowers and savers.

levels.headline: Bank of England keeps rates at 3.75% but three policymakers want a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England kept Bank Rate at 3.75% on 17 September 2026, with the Monetary Policy Committee voting 6 to 3. Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill wanted a rise to 4%.
The committee said risks to inflation lean to the upside and that it is ready to act. It said the Middle East conflict has lifted energy prices and that more increases are expected in the coming quarters.
The majority believed it was better to wait. Inflation was 3.1% in August against a 2% target, with motor fuel a big factor, while core inflation was 2.6%.
Rates have been at 3.75% since a cut in December 2025. The next decision is on 5 November, together with a new Monetary Policy Report, and some forecasters think a rise is increasingly likely if energy prices stay high.
A rise would raise costs for people on variable-rate mortgages and loans, and reward savers.
levels.why: It signals that interest rates could rise soon, which would affect mortgages, loans and savings.

levels.headline: Bank of England leaves interest rates at 3.75%, but the vote is close
levels.body:
The Bank of England decided on 17 September to keep its main interest rate, Bank Rate, at 3.75%. Six members of the Monetary Policy Committee voted to hold. Three, Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill, wanted to raise it to 4%.
The committee warned that the risks to inflation are on the upside and said it is ready to act if needed. It said the conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy prices and that prices may rise further in the coming months.
Inflation, the rate at which prices go up, was 3.1% in August. The Bank aims for 2%. Much of the gap comes from energy, especially petrol and diesel. Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, inflation was 2.6%.
The next decision is on 5 November. If rates go up, people with variable mortgages and loans would pay more, while savers could earn a little more.
levels.why: It affects how much people pay on mortgages and loans, and what savers earn.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay at 3.75%, but some Bank of England members wanted a rise
levels.body:
The Bank of England has kept its main interest rate at 3.75%. The decision was made on 17 September. Nine people on the Monetary Policy Committee vote on it. Six wanted no change. Three wanted to raise the rate to 4%.
The Bank said prices could rise faster than it hopes, and that it is ready to act. It said the war in the Middle East has made energy more expensive, and that this may push prices up further.
In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. The Bank wants this number to be 2%. Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, the number was lower, at 2.6%.
The Bank will decide again on 5 November. If it raises the rate, borrowing gets dearer. People with mortgages that change with the rate would pay more each month. People with savings could earn a little more.
levels.why: Interest rates change what households pay on debt and earn on savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has not changed its interest rate, but some members wanted to
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the country's money system. It sets an interest rate called Bank Rate. This rate affects how much it costs to borrow money and how much savers earn. On 17 September the Bank kept the rate at 3.75%.
Nine people vote on the rate. Six voted to leave it alone. Three voted to put it up to 4%. They are Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill.
The Bank is worried because prices are going up faster than it wants. Prices were 3.1% higher in August than a year earlier. The Bank wants prices to rise by about 2%. A big reason is that energy, like petrol, costs more because of the war in the Middle East.
The Bank will decide again on 5 November. If the rate goes up, loans and some mortgages would cost more.
levels.why: It could change how much families pay each month on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Interest rates stay the same for now, but they may go up
levels.body:
The Bank of England is in charge of one very important number. It is called Bank Rate. It is the interest rate that helps decide how much it costs to borrow money. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. On 17 September the Bank said the rate would stay at 3.75%.
Nine people voted. Six said keep it the same. Three said make it higher. The Bank is worried about inflation. Inflation means prices going up. In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year before. The Bank wants them to go up by only 2%.
Prices are going up mostly because of energy. Petrol, diesel and gas cost more because of fighting in the Middle East.
The Bank will choose again on 5 November. If it makes the rate higher, people who have loans or some mortgages would pay more. People with savings in a bank might get a little extra.
levels.why: It shows prices are still rising too fast, which could make borrowing dearer.

levels.headline: The Bank of England has kept its rate the same, but may raise it later
levels.body:
The Bank of England looks after the money in our country. It chooses an interest rate. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow money. It is also the extra money a bank pays you when you save. On 17 September the Bank decided to keep the rate at 3.75%.
Nine people had a say. Six wanted to keep the rate where it was. Three wanted to make it bigger.
The Bank is worried because prices are going up. This is called inflation. In August, things cost 3.1% more than a year earlier. The Bank would like that number to be 2%. Petrol and gas cost more because of the fighting in the Middle East.
The Bank will decide again on 5 November. If it makes the rate bigger, then borrowing money will cost more. That could be hard for families who have loans or a mortgage. A mortgage is a loan to buy a house.
levels.why: It affects how much families pay when they borrow money.

levels.headline: The Bank of England kept its rate the same, but some members want it higher
levels.body:
The Bank of England is the bank that looks after the country's money. It sets an interest rate called Bank Rate. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow, and the extra money a bank gives you when you save. On 17 September, the Bank decided to keep the rate at 3.75%.
Nine people vote on the rate. Six voted to keep it the same. Three voted to raise it to 4%.
They are worried about inflation, which means prices going up. In August, prices were 3.1% higher than a year earlier. The Bank wants prices to rise by only about 2%. Energy, like petrol and gas, has become more expensive because of the war in the Middle East.
The Bank will choose again on 5 November. If the rate goes up, loans and some mortgages will cost more each month. A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home.
levels.why: It could change how much families pay on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: The Bank has left the rate alone, for now
levels.body:
The Bank of England is a very big bank for the whole country. It decides on a number called the interest rate. Think of it as the price of borrowing money. If you borrow money, you pay a bit extra back. That extra bit is called interest.
On 17 September, the Bank said it would leave the rate at 3.75%. Nine people voted. Six said leave it. Three said make it higher.
Why might it go higher? Because prices are rising. Things in the shops cost more now than they did a year ago. In August, they cost 3.1% more. The Bank wants prices to go up by just 2%. Petrol and gas cost more because of fighting far away.
The Bank will choose again on 5 November. If the rate goes up, people who borrowed money will have to pay back more each month. Saving money could pay a little more.
levels.why: It matters because it changes how much people pay on loans and what savers earn.

levels.headline: Why the Bank is watching prices closely
levels.body:
Imagine you get pocket money every week. Then your favourite sweets start to cost more. Your money buys less than before. That is called inflation, and it is what the Bank of England is worried about.
The Bank of England is a special bank that looks after the country's money. It picks a number called the interest rate. When grown-ups borrow money, they pay extra back, and the interest rate decides how much extra. On 17 September, the Bank kept the number at 3.75%.
Nine people voted. Six said keep it the same. Three said make it a bit bigger, to help stop prices going up too fast.
Prices have gone up more than the Bank would like. Petrol and gas cost more because of fighting far away.
The Bank will choose again on 5 November. If it makes the number bigger, borrowing money costs more.
levels.why: It is about stopping the things we buy from costing more and more.

headline: UK economy grew 0.5% in the second quarter, revised up from 0.4%, leading the G7 in the first half

terms.meaning: Gross domestic product, the total value of goods and services a country produces.
Businesses that sell services rather than goods, such as shops, banks, restaurants and care.
A group of seven large advanced economies, including the UK, US, Japan and Germany.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.5% in the second quarter, revised up from 0.4%, leading the G7 in the first half
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics revised UK economic growth for April to June 2026 up to 0.5%, from a first estimate of 0.4%, in its quarterly national accounts published on 30 September.
Growth in the first quarter was left unchanged at 0.6%, which means the UK was the fastest growing of the G7 large advanced economies in the first half of the year. Output in the second quarter was 1.4% higher than a year earlier, up from an initial estimate of 1.2%.
Services drove the upgrade. ONS statistics director Liz McKeown said stronger service-sector growth meant the economy is slightly larger than previously thought. Construction grew 0.8% while production fell 0.1%. Business investment growth was revised up to an annual rate of 5.2% from 0.8%, and real household disposable income per head rose 1.0%.
Economists said the figures suggest the economy has been more resilient to higher energy prices than expected, though they warned that inflation pressures from energy and geopolitical conflicts could slow growth in the second half. The next quarterly accounts are due on 12 November, a fortnight after the Budget.
levels.why: Stronger growth means more tax revenue and jobs, and gives the Chancellor more room ahead of the Budget.

levels.headline: UK growth revised up to 0.5% for April to June
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics said on 30 September that the UK economy grew by 0.5% in April to June 2026, up from its first estimate of 0.4%.
First-quarter growth stayed at 0.6%, so the UK grew faster than any other G7 economy in the first half of 2026. Output was 1.4% higher than a year earlier, compared with an earlier estimate of 1.2%.
The revision came mainly from services. Liz McKeown of the ONS said the economy is slightly bigger than previously estimated. Construction rose 0.8% and production fell 0.1%. Business investment growth was revised to an annual 5.2% from 0.8%, and real household disposable income per head grew 1.0%.
One economist quoted by Reuters said the economy had been more resilient to energy price rises than thought. Others warned that energy costs and geopolitical conflicts could slow growth later in the year.
The ONS will publish its next quarterly figures on 12 November.
levels.why: It shows the economy is stronger than first thought, although risks remain for the second half of the year.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew faster than first thought in spring

The UK economy grew by 0.5% between April and June 2026, according to new figures from the Office for National Statistics. The first estimate had been 0.4%.

Most of the extra growth came from services, such as shops, banks and restaurants. The ONS said the economy is slightly larger than it had thought. Building work grew 0.8%, while factories and other production fell 0.1%. Companies also invested more than first estimated, and the average person's income after tax and prices rose 1.0%.
Economists said the economy handled high energy prices better than expected, but warned that conflict and energy costs could slow it in the second half.
The next update is on 12 November.
levels.why: A growing economy supports jobs, wages and the public finances.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.5% in spring, up from first estimate of 0.4%

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a little more than thought in the spring
levels.body:
New figures show the UK economy grew by 0.5% from April to June 2026. Earlier, the official number was 0.4%. The Office for National Statistics, which counts these things, changed it on 30 September.
The economy grew 0.6% in the first three months of the year. Across the first six months, the UK grew faster than any other country in the G7, a group of seven large, rich countries. Compared with a year ago, the economy is 1.4% bigger.

Businesses also spent more on things like machines and buildings, and the money people had left to spend grew by 1.0% per person.
Some experts said the economy dealt well with higher energy costs. Others warned that things could slow down later in the year.
levels.why: It shows whether the country is getting richer, which affects jobs and wages.

levels.headline: Britain's economy grew by a bit more than people first said
levels.body:
The economy is all the things people make, sell and buy in a country. Experts measure how much it grows. They looked at April to June 2026 and found the economy grew by 0.5%. They had first said 0.4%, so it was a little better.
In the first three months it grew by 0.6%. That means the UK grew faster than any of the other big rich countries in a group called the G7, over the first half of the year. Over a whole year, it grew by 1.4%.
Most of the growth came from services. Services are jobs where people do things for other people, like shops, banks and cafes. Building grew by 0.8%. Factories made a bit less than before. Businesses spent more on new machines and buildings, and families had a little more money to spend.
Some experts say the economy did better than expected, even with energy costing more. Others think growth might slow down later this year.
levels.why: A bigger economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: The country is making and selling a bit more than before

levels.why: When the economy grows, there can be more jobs and more money to spend.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a bit more than experts first said

levels.headline: The country's money machine grew a little

A country has a kind of money machine. It is called the economy. It is all the work people do and all the things they buy and sell. Every few months, experts check if it has got bigger or smaller. This time they found it grew by 0.5% from April to June. They had first said 0.4%.

levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and more money for everyone.

levels.headline: The country got a bit richer this spring

Think of the whole country as one big shop and workplace. Everything that people make and sell and all the work they do adds up to something called the economy. Experts check each season to see if it has grown bigger.
From April to June, they said it grew by a small bit: 0.5%. That is tiny, like a plant growing half a centimetre. At first they thought it was a bit smaller, but they checked again.
The UK grew faster than other big, rich countries in the first half of the year. That is a bit like finishing first in a race.
Most of the growth came from people doing jobs for others, like working in shops, banks and cafes. People also had slightly more money to spend.

levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and money for schools and hospitals.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% and the energy price cap goes up 4% from October

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
Ofgem's limit on the price per unit of gas and electricity that suppliers can charge.
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.1% and the energy price cap goes up 4% from October
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, from 2.9% in July, the highest in five months and in line with market expectations. Transport was the biggest upward pressure, with transport inflation rising to 4.6% from 3.6%, driven particularly by motor fuels. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, held at 2.6% for a second month.
On 26 August Ofgem announced that its price cap would rise by 4% for 1 October to 31 December. The typical dual-fuel bill goes from £1,663 to £1,723 a year, about £5 a month more. The rise is driven almost entirely by gas, which is up 8%, while electricity is broadly stable because of a government decision to remove VAT on domestic electricity bills. Part of the headline reflects a change to Ofgem's assumptions about typical use.
The Bank of England blames the rise in inflation on the Middle East conflict and its effect on energy prices. The next cap, covering January to March 2027, will be announced on 25 November. Cornwall Insight has forecast a rise, with one projection putting the cap at £1,872. September inflation figures are due on 21 October.
levels.why: Rising bills and prices squeeze household budgets and feed into decisions on interest rates and benefits.

levels.headline: Inflation hits 3.1% and the October energy cap rises by 4%
levels.body:
UK inflation rose to 3.1% in the year to August 2026, up from 2.9% in July. It was the highest rate in five months and matched forecasts. Transport costs pushed it up most, with transport inflation at 4.6% compared with 3.6% in July, mainly because of motor fuels. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, stayed at 2.6%.
Ofgem said on 26 August that the energy price cap would rise by 4% from 1 October to 31 December. A typical dual-fuel bill rises from £1,663 to £1,723 a year, about £5 a month. Gas costs are up 8%, but electricity is steady because VAT on domestic electricity was removed. Some of the headline change comes from new assumptions about typical household use.
The Bank of England says the Middle East conflict has raised energy prices and inflation. The next cap will be announced on 25 November, and forecasters at Cornwall Insight expect it to rise. The September inflation figure is due on 21 October.
levels.why: Higher energy bills and prices reduce what households can spend and shape interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and energy bills go up again in October
levels.body:
UK inflation, the rate at which prices rise, was 3.1% in the year to August 2026. In July it was 2.9%. This was the highest level for five months. Transport costs rose fastest, mainly because of petrol and diesel. Without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, inflation was 2.6%, the same as the month before.
The regulator Ofgem has raised its energy price cap by 4% for October to December. The price cap limits what suppliers can charge per unit of energy. A typical household will pay £1,723 a year instead of £1,663, which is about £5 a month more. Gas is 8% dearer, while electricity prices are steady because the government took VAT off domestic electricity bills.
The Bank of England says the conflict in the Middle East has pushed up energy prices. The next price cap will be announced on 25 November and forecasters expect another rise. The next inflation figure comes on 21 October.
levels.why: It affects what families pay for fuel, food and heating this winter.

levels.headline: Prices rose 3.1% in a year and energy bills are going up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.1% higher in August than a year earlier. This is called inflation. In July it was 2.9%, so it has gone up. It is the highest in five months. Petrol and diesel were a big reason. If you leave out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose 2.6%.
Energy bills are going up too. The energy price cap is a limit set by a regulator called Ofgem on what companies can charge for each unit of gas and electricity. From 1 October the cap rose by 4%. A typical home will pay £1,723 a year, up from £1,663. That is about £5 a month more. Gas costs more, but electricity does not because the government took VAT off it.
The Bank of England says the war in the Middle East is making energy dearer. The cap will change again in January, and experts think it will rise. The next list of prices comes out on 21 October.
levels.why: Many families will find food, fuel and heating more expensive.

levels.headline: Things cost more, and heating bills are going up
levels.body:
Prices in the UK went up by 3.1% over the year to August. When prices rise like this, it is called inflation. In July the figure was 2.9%, so it is higher now. Petrol and diesel were a big reason.
Energy bills are rising too. There is a limit on how much energy companies can charge for each unit of gas or electricity. It is called the price cap. A regulator called Ofgem sets it. From 1 October the cap went up by 4%. A normal home will now pay about £1,723 a year for energy. Before it was £1,663. That is about £5 more a month. Gas costs more. Electricity costs about the same, because the government took a tax called VAT off it.
The Bank of England says fighting in the Middle East has made energy dearer around the world. The cap will change again in January. Experts think it could go up. We will see the next price figures on 21 October.
levels.why: Families have to find more money for the same things.

levels.headline: Prices keep going up, and so do energy bills
levels.body:
Prices in the shops are going up. In the year to August, they went up by 3.1%. This is called inflation. In July it was 2.9%, so the number has grown. Petrol and diesel cost a lot more, and this is a big reason.
Energy bills are going up too. Energy companies cannot charge as much as they like. A group called Ofgem puts a limit on what they can charge. This is called the price cap. From 1 October the limit went up by 4%. A normal home will pay about £1,723 a year for gas and electricity. It used to be £1,663. That is around £5 more each month.
Gas is more expensive. Electricity costs about the same because the government took off a tax called VAT.
The Bank of England says fighting in the Middle East is making energy dear all over the world. The cap will change again in January, and it may go up again.
levels.why: It means a bit less money is left over for other things.

levels.headline: Why things in the shops cost more now
levels.body:
Prices go up over time, but this year they have gone up faster. In August, things cost 3.1% more than they did a year before. This is called inflation. So something that cost £10 last year would now cost about £10.31.
One big reason is energy. Energy means things like petrol for cars and gas to heat homes. Fighting in the Middle East has made energy cost more all over the world.
Heating bills are going up too. A group called Ofgem decides how much energy companies can charge. This is the price cap. From 1 October it went up by 4%. A normal home will pay about £5 more each month for gas and electricity. Gas costs more. Electricity costs about the same, because the government took off a tax.
Next time the cap will change is in January. Experts think it could go up again.
levels.why: Higher prices mean families can buy less with the same money.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster and energy bills are rising
levels.body:
Prices in the shops are going up. In the year to August they rose by 3.1%. This is called inflation. It was 2.9% in July, so it has gone up. Petrol and diesel were a big part of the reason.
Energy bills are rising too. A regulator called Ofgem sets a limit on what energy companies can charge for each unit of gas or electricity. This is called the price cap. From 1 October the cap went up by 4%. A normal home will pay about £1,723 a year for gas and electricity, instead of £1,663. That is about £5 more each month.
Gas costs more. Electricity costs about the same, because the government took off a tax called VAT.

levels.why: It means families can buy a little less with the same money.

levels.headline: Things in the shops cost a bit more than before
levels.body:
Do you remember when a bar of chocolate cost less? Over the last year, most things have got a little more expensive. In August, things cost 3.1% more than a year ago. That is about 3 pence more for every pound. We call this inflation.
Petrol for cars costs more. Gas that keeps houses warm costs more too. This is because there is fighting a long way away, in a part of the world called the Middle East. A lot of the world's energy comes from there.
There is a limit on how much companies can charge for energy at home. This limit is going up a little from October. A normal family will pay about £5 more each month.
Grown-ups are worried about this, because their money does not go as far. People who decide things are watching closely.
levels.why: It makes grown-ups' money go less far.

levels.headline: Why your family might feel the pinch
levels.body:
Imagine your pocket money stays the same, but sweets cost a bit more each month. You can buy less. That is what grown-ups are feeling. Prices of lots of things have gone up a little over the last year. About 3 pence more for every pound. The grown-up word for this is inflation.
One reason is that energy costs more. Energy is what makes cars go and keeps houses warm. There is fighting far away, and that makes energy dearer.
There is a limit on how much energy companies can charge. It has gone up a bit too. A normal family will pay about £5 more each month to heat their home.
That is not a lot, but it adds up. People in charge are watching to see if prices keep rising.
levels.why: It is like sweets costing more when your pocket money stays the same.

headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as payrolled jobs fall over the year

terms.meaning: The share of people who are looking for work and available to start, among everyone who is working or looking.
People recorded as being paid through company payrolls, using tax records.
The system of jobs, workers and employers in an economy.

levels.headline: UK unemployment holds at 4.9% as payrolled jobs fall over the year
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate for people aged 16 and over was 4.9% in May to July 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics release of 15 September. The ONS put the number of unemployed people at about 1.78 million. The rate was the same as the 4.9% recorded for April to June, so it was flat between the two releases. The male rate was 5.3% and the female rate 4.5%.
Tax records show a weaker picture for employers' payrolls. The number of payrolled employees fell by 101,000, or 0.3%, between July 2025 and July 2026, and by 19,000, or 0.1%, between June and July 2026. Early estimates for August showed payrolled employees down by 145,000, or 0.5%, on the year at 30.2 million, though the ONS warns that early estimates are often revised.
The labour market figures matter to the Bank of England, which considers pay and jobs when it sets interest rates. The Treasury's September consensus of forecasters expects unemployment of around 5.1% by the end of the year. The next labour market figures are due on 20 October, eight days before the Budget.
levels.why: Jobs data shapes interest rate decisions and shows how secure work feels for ordinary people.

levels.headline: Unemployment steady at 4.9% but payrolled employment is falling
levels.body:
UK unemployment was 4.9% in the three months from May to July 2026, the ONS reported on 15 September. That is the same as in the April to June period. About 1.78 million people were unemployed. Men had a rate of 5.3% and women 4.5%.
Tax records show falling payrolls. Payrolled employees fell by 101,000, or 0.3%, between July 2025 and July 2026, and by 19,000 between June and July. Early figures for August suggested a drop of 145,000, or 0.5%, over the year, to 30.2 million, but these are often revised.
The Bank of England watches jobs and pay closely when it sets interest rates. The Treasury's September survey of forecasters expects unemployment to be around 5.1% by the end of the year.
The next figures are due on 20 October, a week before the Budget.
levels.why: A weak jobs market affects incomes and also affects whether interest rates rise or fall.

levels.headline: Unemployment stays at 4.9%, but fewer people are on company payrolls
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% from May to July 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics. That was the same as the figure for April to June. Around 1.78 million people were out of work and looking for a job. The rate was higher for men, at 5.3%, than for women, at 4.5%.
Tax records show fewer people being paid by employers. The number of payrolled employees fell by 101,000, or 0.3%, between July 2025 and July 2026. It dropped by 19,000 between June and July alone. Early figures for August suggested a bigger fall, but the ONS says these early numbers are often changed later.
The Bank of England looks at jobs and wages when it decides on interest rates. Forecasters surveyed by the Treasury expect unemployment of about 5.1% by the end of the year.
New figures are due on 20 October.
levels.why: It shows how easy it is to find and keep a job.

levels.headline: Around 1.8 million people in the UK are out of work
levels.body:
The UK unemployment rate was 4.9% from May to July 2026. This means about 5 in every 100 people who want to work could not find a job. Around 1.78 million people were in that position. The rate was 5.3% for men and 4.5% for women. It was the same as the figure for the months before.
Tax records give another picture. They count people who are paid through a company payroll. In July, there were 101,000 fewer than a year earlier. That is a fall of 0.3%. Between June and July, it fell by 19,000.
The Bank of England looks at jobs and pay when deciding about interest rates. Forecasters think unemployment will go up a little, to about 5.1%, by the end of the year.
The next figures come out on 20 October.
levels.why: If jobs are harder to find, people have less money to spend and less security.

levels.headline: About 5 in every 100 people who want a job cannot find one
levels.body:
In the UK, 4.9% of people who want to work did not have a job from May to July 2026. That is about 5 in every 100 people. It is around 1.78 million people. For men the number was 5.3%. For women it was 4.5%. This was the same as the months before.
There is a second way to count jobs. It uses tax records of people paid by companies. This count showed 101,000 fewer people on company payrolls in July than a year earlier. That is a fall of 0.3%.
The Bank of England looks at how many people have jobs when it decides how high interest rates should be. Experts think that unemployment could rise a little, to about 5.1%, by the end of the year.
The next set of job figures comes on 20 October.
levels.why: A job gives people money to live on, so more people without work is worrying.

levels.headline: More than a million and a half people are looking for a job
levels.body:
A person is counted as unemployed if they do not have a job but want one and are looking for work. In the UK, between May and July, about 5 in every 100 people who wanted to work did not have a job. That is 4.9%. It is about 1.78 million people. It was the same number as before.
There is another count too. The government can see how many people are paid by companies through tax records. In July this number was 101,000 lower than a year before. That means fewer people had a paid job with a company.
The Bank of England watches this closely. It uses job numbers to decide on interest rates.
Some experts think that the number of people without jobs could go up a bit by the end of the year, to about 5.1%.
The next numbers are due on 20 October.
levels.why: More people without jobs means less money in people's homes.

levels.headline: Some grown-ups cannot find work
levels.body:
Most grown-ups have jobs. A job is work that you do to earn money. But some people cannot find one, even though they want one. These people are called unemployed. Between May and July, about 5 in every 100 grown-ups who wanted to work did not have a job. That is a lot of people. It is about 1.78 million in all.
The numbers are about the same as they were a few months ago. But there is another way of counting. The government can look at tax records to see how many people are paid by companies. There were 101,000 fewer people on these lists in July than a year before.
Experts at the Bank of England keep an eye on jobs. They use the numbers to help decide on interest rates.
Some experts think the number of people without a job might go up a little by the end of the year.
levels.why: People without jobs have less money to spend on food and bills.

levels.headline: About 5 in every 100 people who want a job cannot find one
levels.body:
A person counts as unemployed if they do not have a job, want one and are looking for work. From May to July, 4.9% of people who wanted to work in the UK did not have a job. That is about 5 in every 100 people, or around 1.78 million people. The number was the same as before.
There is another way to count. The government can look at tax records to see how many people are paid by companies. In July there were 101,000 fewer than a year earlier.
The Bank of England looks at job numbers when it decides about interest rates. Some experts think the number of people without jobs could go up a little, to about 5.1%, by the end of the year.
The next job figures are out on 20 October.
levels.why: Jobs give people the money to pay for food and homes.

levels.headline: Some people who want a job cannot find one
levels.body:
Lots of grown-ups go to work and get paid. That is called having a job. Some grown-ups want a job but cannot find one. They are called unemployed.
Experts counted them. They found that about 5 out of every 100 grown-ups who wanted to work did not have a job. If you had 100 people in a big hall, about 5 of them would be looking for work. In the whole country, that is a very large number: about 1.78 million people.
The number is about the same as it was a few months ago. But companies are paying slightly fewer people than a year ago.
Grown-ups who decide on money matters keep an eye on this. If more people do not have jobs, they have to think about what to do to help.
levels.why: Everyone needs money for food and a home, so jobs matter.

levels.headline: Why grown-ups worry about jobs
levels.body:
Most grown-ups go to work to earn money. They use the money to buy food and pay for a home. A few grown-ups want to work but cannot find a job. These grown-ups are called unemployed.
Imagine a classroom of 20 grown-ups who all want a job. About 1 of them would not be able to find one. In the whole country, about 1.78 million people are in this position.
It is about the same number as a few months ago. But companies are paying a few thousand fewer people than a year ago.
The people who look after the country's money watch this carefully. If fewer people have jobs, they think about ways to help.
The next numbers come out on 20 October.
levels.why: Having a job helps families pay for food and homes.

headline: Russian missile and drone barrage kills at least 30 across Ukraine, including 22 in Pryluky

terms.meaning: A guided missile that flies low and can travel a long way to hit a target.
Power stations, grids and gas systems that supply electricity and heat.
A loss of electric power across an area.

levels.headline: Russian missile and drone barrage kills at least 30 across Ukraine, including 22 in Pryluky
levels.body:
Russia launched a large missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into 7 October 2026, killing at least 30 people and injuring more than 100, according to Ukrainian officials. The strikes fell on Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia fired about 70 missiles along with drones, and the Ukrainian air force counted around 130 drones, including decoys. Energy infrastructure was among the main targets. Russia's Defence Ministry said it hit Ukraine's defence industry.
The deadliest single strike hit Pryluky, a city in the Chernihiv region, where a cruise missile destroyed a five-storey apartment block. The regional governor put the death toll there at 22, including five children, with more than 50 injured, and warned people could still be trapped in the rubble. Figures were still changing.
Overnight into 8 October, drones hit districts of Kyiv and killed four people, according to NPR and the Associated Press. Blackouts have worsened in the capital. Zelensky warned that missile and drone attacks are likely to intensify as winter approaches, as Russia targets the power system that provides heat and light.
levels.why: Attacks on homes and power supplies put civilians at risk and show the war is still intensifying before winter.

levels.headline: Russia hits Ukraine with about 70 missiles and 130 drones, killing at least 30
levels.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine overnight into 7 October 2026 with about 70 missiles and some 130 drones, including decoys, according to President Zelensky and the Ukrainian air force. At least 30 people were killed and more than 100 injured, the Kyiv Independent reported. The date was Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region, a cruise missile destroyed a five-storey apartment block. The governor said 22 people died, including five children, and more than 50 were hurt. Rescuers feared more people were trapped.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it targeted Ukraine's defence industry, while Zelensky said energy infrastructure was among the main targets. Overnight into 8 October, drones hit Kyiv and killed four people, NPR and AP reported.
Blackouts in Kyiv have worsened. Zelensky warned that attacks will probably grow as winter nears.
levels.why: Civilian deaths and damage to power networks matter for Ukraine's winter and for peace efforts.

levels.headline: Russian strikes kill at least 30 in Ukraine, 22 of them in one apartment block
levels.body:
Ukrainian officials say a Russian attack overnight into 7 October killed at least 30 people across Ukraine and injured over 100. Russia used around 70 missiles and about 130 drones, many of them decoys. It happened on Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.

headline: Lithuania's parliament backs lifting ban on hosting nuclear weapons at first vote; Kremlin warns of escalation

terms.meaning: A military alliance of 32 countries, including the UK, US and Lithuania, that agree to defend each other.
A rule written into a country's constitution that can only be changed by a special vote.
A step-by-step increase in tension or conflict.

levels.headline: Lithuania's parliament backs lifting ban on hosting nuclear weapons at first vote; Kremlin warns of escalation
levels.body:
Lithuania's parliament took a first step on 6 October 2026 towards removing a constitutional ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its territory, passing the first reading of the bill by 106 votes to 18. The Kremlin responded the same day, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying the move could lead to a new round of escalation in the region.
The bill needs a second vote after a mandatory three-month wait. That final vote is tentatively scheduled for 12 January 2027 and requires a two-thirds majority, meaning at least 94 of the 141 members. Lithuania is a member of NATO and borders Russia's Kaliningrad region and Belarus.
Lithuanian officials stress that changing the law does not mean weapons will be deployed. Vilnius has said there are currently no plans to station them.
Peskov linked the vote to a proposal floated this month by US President Donald Trump to build an American military base in Lithuania. He said that if NATO military infrastructure moves closer to Russia's borders it cannot be seen as anything but a step towards escalating tensions, and that Russia would take all necessary measures to ensure its own security. Earlier Russian warnings had been harsher; Kyiv Post described his latest remarks as milder.
levels.why: It shows how nuclear weapons are re-entering debates in Europe as tensions with Russia grow.

levels.headline: Lithuanian MPs back first step to lift nuclear weapons ban, Kremlin warns of escalation

Officials in Vilnius say the change would not mean weapons are deployed and that there are no current plans to station them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also referred to a proposal by President Trump this month to build a US military base in Lithuania. He said bringing NATO infrastructure closer to Russia's border increases tension and that Russia would take all necessary measures for its security. Kyiv Post said his remarks were milder than earlier Russian threats.
levels.why: Nuclear policy on NATO's eastern edge affects security across Europe, including the UK.

levels.headline: Lithuania moves to lift its ban on nuclear weapons; Russia warns of escalation

Russian spokesman Dmitry Peskov also mentioned an idea from President Trump for a US military base in Lithuania. He said moving NATO forces closer to Russia's borders is a step towards more tension and that Russia would take whatever steps it needed to stay safe.
levels.why: It shows how tension between NATO and Russia is shaping decisions in countries near Russia.

headline: Fresh Iranian attacks on tankers deepen Hormuz crisis as US-Iran diplomacy remains stalled

terms.meaning: A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of the world's oil and gas normally passes.

levels.headline: Fresh Iranian attacks on tankers deepen Hormuz crisis as US-Iran diplomacy remains stalled
levels.body:
Attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into October 2026, deepening a crisis that has run for about six months and kept diplomacy between the United States and Iran stalled.
Bloomberg reported on 7 October that fresh tanker attacks by Iran were threatening a recent recovery in Middle East oil flows. UK Maritime Trade Operations had reported at least nine attacks in the waterway so far in October. Shipments through the strait had risen in recent weeks, but the pace of Iranian strikes on ships has also increased.
The diplomatic picture is difficult. On 18 August, President Trump said there were no talks planned with Iran and that the US naval blockade of Iranian ports remained in full force. Iran has said the strait will not reopen until Washington ends the blockade, and it has held talks with Oman about a temporary shipping corridor. The Revolutionary Guard has been turning back vessels that use routes it has not approved, and Iran wants control of the strait, including the right to charge fees, which Washington rejects.
About a fifth of the world's oil and gas normally passes through the strait, so the dispute affects energy prices around the world, including UK fuel and gas bills.
levels.why: The standoff keeps oil and gas prices high, which feeds into inflation and household bills in the UK.

headline: Oil jumps back above $100 as fresh Iranian tanker attacks threaten supply

levels.headline: Oil jumps back above $100 as fresh Iranian tanker attacks threaten supply
levels.body:
Oil prices jumped on 7 October 2026 after new attacks on tankers by Iran, with Brent crude climbing as much as 5.7%, its biggest intraday rise in nearly a month. Bloomberg reported the price topping $105 a barrel at the peak, though other price trackers showed Brent a little above $100 later in the day.
Brent had settled near $101 on 6 October, while the US benchmark West Texas Intermediate traded below $90 after a volatile session.
Two factors drove the rise. Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz had increased in recent weeks, but the pace of Iranian strikes on ships rose too. UK Maritime Trade Operations has reported at least nine attacks in the waterway this month. Separately, the first Atlantic hurricane of the year cut oil production in the US Gulf, and soaring freight rates are adding to the cost of moving oil.
Prices were about $70 before the Middle East war began, and reached around $115 in early May. For the UK, higher oil prices feed through to petrol and diesel prices and to inflation, which the Bank of England says is being driven by energy costs.
levels.why: Oil prices influence petrol costs, inflation and interest rates, so they affect nearly every household.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because of fighting far away

levels.headline: Why fuel is costing more
levels.body:
Imagine a sweet shop. If the sweets cannot get to the shop, there are fewer to sell. The shop might put the price up, because the sweets are harder to get.
Oil is like that. Oil is a dark liquid. We use it to make petrol for cars and buses. A lot of oil is carried on big ships near a place called Iran. This week, some of those ships were attacked. People worried there would not be enough oil. So the price of oil went up.

levels.why: When something is harder to get, it usually costs more.

headline: US 10-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2002 on inflation and deficit worries

terms.meaning: The interest rate the US government pays to borrow money, which sets a benchmark for other borrowing costs.
A loan to a government or company that pays interest and is repaid later.
A sale where the government offers new bonds to investors, who bid to buy them.

levels.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield hits highest level since 2002 on inflation and deficit worries
levels.body:
The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note rose to its highest level since 2002 on 7 October 2026, with reports putting the peak at about 5.34% to 5.36% before it eased later in the day. The 30-year yield also reached a multi-decade high, near 5.70%, earlier in the week.
A yield is the return investors demand for lending to the government, and it rises when bond prices fall. The move reflects worries about inflation, which has been pushed up by higher energy prices linked to the conflict with Iran, and about government borrowing. Forbes cited a projected federal deficit of $1.9 trillion, alongside heavy borrowing by technology firms for artificial intelligence.
Markets were also waiting for a $39 billion auction of 10-year notes on 7 October, seen as a test of investor demand, and for minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting.
The 10-year yield is a benchmark for borrowing costs across the economy. Forbes reported that the average 30-year fixed US mortgage rate rose from 7.30% to 7.49%. Because US yields influence global markets, they also affect UK government borrowing costs and the Chancellor's room for manoeuvre ahead of the Budget.
levels.why: US borrowing costs set the tone for mortgages and loans worldwide, including in the UK.

levels.headline: US 10-year Treasury yield reaches 24-year high above 5.3%
levels.body:

The yield is what investors demand to lend to the US government. It rises when bond prices fall. Analysts linked the move to inflation fears, partly driven by energy prices during the conflict with Iran, and to concerns over borrowing. Forbes pointed to a projected federal deficit of $1.9 trillion and heavy borrowing by technology firms for AI.
Investors were watching a $39 billion 10-year note auction and the minutes of the Fed's September meeting.
The average 30-year US mortgage rate rose from 7.30% to 7.49%, according to Forbes. US yields also influence government borrowing costs elsewhere, including the UK.
levels.why: Rising yields make mortgages and business loans dearer and affect governments' borrowing costs everywhere.

levels.body:
The interest rate on 10-year US government bonds rose to about 5.34% to 5.36% on 7 October 2026. That is the highest since 2002. It fell back a little later in the day. The 30-year rate also hit a level not seen for decades, near 5.70%, earlier in the week.

levels.why: It makes borrowing dearer for homebuyers and businesses, and it affects other countries' borrowing costs.

levels.headline: US 10-year yield rises to highest since 2002
levels.body:
The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds climbed to around 5.34% to 5.36% on 7 October, the highest since 2002, before easing later in the day. The 30-year yield reached around 5.70% earlier in the week, also a multi-decade high.
