levels.why: Rising US yields push up borrowing costs around the world.

levels.headline: The cost of borrowing for the US government is the highest in over 20 years
levels.body:
The interest rate on US government 10-year bonds rose to about 5.35% on 7 October. This is the highest it has been since 2002. It dropped back a little later in the day. The rate on 30-year bonds also rose to about 5.70% earlier in the week.
This rate is called a yield. A bond is a loan that investors make to the government. The yield is the interest they earn. It goes up when investors do not want to buy the bonds.
Analysts say investors are worried about prices rising, partly because energy costs more during the conflict with Iran. They are also worried about how much the government is borrowing. Forbes said the deficit could be $1.9 trillion this year.
Home loans cost more too. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in the US rose from 7.30% to 7.49%.
levels.why: It makes loans and mortgages dearer and can affect other countries too.

levels.headline: US government borrowing costs hit a 24-year high
levels.body:
The cost of borrowing for the US government hit its highest level since 2002 on 7 October. The rate on 10-year bonds reached about 5.35% before falling back a bit. The rate on 30-year bonds also reached about 5.70% earlier in the week.
A bond is a loan to the government. When you buy a bond, you lend the government money and it pays you interest. The yield is that interest. It goes up when fewer people want to buy bonds.
Some experts say investors are worried that prices will keep rising, partly because energy costs more because of the Iran conflict. They are also worried about how much money the government is borrowing. One report said the deficit might be $1.9 trillion.
Home loans in the US cost more as a result. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose from 7.30% to 7.49%.
levels.why: It means loans cost more, and it also affects other countries.

levels.headline: It costs the US government more to borrow money
levels.body:
When a government wants more money, it can borrow from people and companies. It sells them something called a bond. A bond is a promise to pay the money back later with extra on top. The extra is called interest. The yield is the rate of interest.
On 7 October, the yield on 10-year US bonds hit about 5.35%. That is the highest since 2002. It fell back a little later in the day. The yield on 30-year bonds also reached about 5.70% earlier in the week.
Yields go up when fewer people want to buy bonds. Some experts say people are worried about prices rising, partly because energy costs more. They also worry that the government is borrowing a lot.
Home loans cost more too. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in the US went from 7.30% to 7.49%.
levels.why: It makes loans dearer for families and firms, and other countries feel it too.

levels.headline: The US government has to pay more to borrow money
levels.body:
Sometimes a government needs more money than it has. So it borrows. It sells something called a bond to people and companies. A bond is a promise to pay the money back later, with some extra. The extra is called interest.
On 7 October, the extra the US government had to pay to borrow for 10 years hit about 5.35%. That is the highest it has been since 2002. It is called the yield.
Why is it going up? Some experts say people are worried that prices will keep rising, partly because oil and gas cost more because of the Iran conflict. Others say the government is borrowing a very large amount.
This affects ordinary people. Loans to buy homes in the US cost more. The usual mortgage rate went from 7.30% to 7.49%.
levels.why: When the government pays more to borrow, banks charge families more too.

levels.headline: It costs more for a big country to borrow money
levels.body:
Sometimes a country needs more money than it has. So it borrows money from people. It gives them a promise to pay the money back later, with some extra on top. The extra is called interest.
The United States is the biggest country economy in the world. This week, the extra it has to pay for borrowing went up. It is the highest it has been for more than 20 years.
Why? Some people are worried that things in shops will keep getting dearer. Oil and gas cost more because of fighting in the Middle East. Other people are worried that the country is borrowing a lot of money.
This matters to ordinary families. People who want to buy a house in the United States have to pay more extra on their home loans too.
levels.why: Families have to pay more when borrowing money for a house.

levels.headline: When borrowing gets dearer
levels.body:
Imagine you borrow £10 from a friend. You say you will give back £11 next week. The extra £1 is the friend's reward for waiting. In grown-up words, the extra is called interest.
Countries borrow money too, from lots of people. This week, the biggest country in the world, the United States, had to promise to pay back a lot more extra than it has for over 20 years. That is because people are worried. They think things in shops might keep getting dearer, and they see that the country is borrowing a lot.
This matters for families. Grown-ups who want to buy a house borrow money too. When borrowing costs more, they have to pay back more.
Grown-ups all over the world are watching closely.
levels.why: When borrowing gets dearer, buying things like houses gets harder.

headline: Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signals more to come

terms.meaning: The US central bank, which sets the main US interest rate.
A rise in the central bank's main interest rate, making borrowing more expensive.
Elections held halfway through a US president's term, to choose Congress.

levels.headline: Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signals more to come
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point on 16 September 2026, to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. The decision of the Federal Open Market Committee was unanimous, and it was the Fed's first rate rise since 2023.
The move defied President Donald Trump, who had demanded cuts. Chair Kevin Warsh described the decision as serious and responsible, and an analysis from MUFG said he framed it as removing accommodation rather than tightening policy. The rise was widely expected after a hot August inflation reading.
The Fed also signalled that more increases may follow. Its projections show the policy rate rising to a range of 4.00% to 4.25% by the end of the year, and markets were pricing roughly a 90% chance of another quarter-point rise by then. The next decision is due on 28 October.
Inflation has been pushed up by energy prices linked to the conflict with Iran. The decision came less than two months before the US midterm elections, and comes as US government bond yields have risen to their highest levels since 2002. Minutes from the September meeting were due on 7 October.
levels.why: The Fed's decisions affect borrowing costs and markets worldwide, including the Bank of England's choices.

levels.headline: Fed raises rates to 3.75%-4.00%, its first rise since 2023
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% on 16 September 2026. The vote was unanimous and it was the Fed's first increase since 2023.
The decision went against President Trump's call for cuts. Chair Kevin Warsh called the move serious and responsible. The hike was expected after a hot reading for August inflation.
The Fed signalled further increases. Its projections show the rate reaching 4.00% to 4.25% by the end of the year, and markets saw about a 90% chance of another quarter-point rise by then. The next meeting ends on 28 October.
Energy prices linked to the Iran conflict have pushed inflation up. The decision came less than two months before the midterm elections. Minutes of the September meeting were due out on 7 October.
levels.why: Higher US rates raise borrowing costs globally and shape central banks' choices elsewhere.

levels.headline: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time in almost three years
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve raised its main interest rate on 16 September 2026 by 0.25 percentage points, to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. All members voted for it. It was the first rise since 2023.
President Donald Trump had asked for lower rates, so the decision went against him. The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, called it a serious and responsible decision. The rise was largely expected after a high inflation figure for August.
The Fed said more rises may follow. Its forecasts show the rate going up to between 4.00% and 4.25% by the end of the year. Investors thought there was about a 90% chance of another rise by then. The next decision is on 28 October.
Prices have been pushed up by energy costs linked to the conflict with Iran. The decision came less than two months before US midterm elections.
levels.why: It affects the cost of loans and mortgages and puts pressure on other central banks.

levels.headline: The US central bank puts up interest rates

The US Federal Reserve, the country's central bank, put up its main interest rate on 16 September. It rose by a quarter of a percentage point, to between 3.75% and 4.00%. Everyone who voted agreed. This is the first rise since 2023.
President Donald Trump wanted rates to come down, so the decision went against him. The Fed's chair is Kevin Warsh. He called the decision serious and responsible. The rise was expected, because prices went up quickly in August.
The Fed said more rises could follow. It thinks rates could reach between 4.00% and 4.25% by the end of the year. Investors thought this was about 90% likely. The next decision is on 28 October.
Prices have been rising partly because oil and gas cost more because of the Iran conflict.
levels.why: Higher rates make loans dearer in the US and can affect borrowing costs in other countries.

levels.headline: America's central bank raises its interest rate

levels.headline: The US puts up its interest rate for the first time since 2023
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve is the US central bank. It sets the main interest rate for the United States. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. On 16 September the Fed raised the rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to between 3.75% and 4.00%. Everyone who voted said yes. It is the first rise since 2023.
The US president, Donald Trump, wanted the rate to go down, so he did not like it. The head of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said it was a serious and responsible choice. The Fed raised the rate because prices were going up too fast.
The Fed said it might raise rates again before the end of the year. The next decision is on 28 October.
Prices have been rising partly because oil and gas cost more.
levels.why: It makes borrowing cost more in the US.

levels.headline: The US raises its interest rate to slow down rising prices
levels.body:
Every country has a central bank. It looks after the money system. The one in the United States is called the Federal Reserve. It chooses a number called the interest rate. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. On 16 September the Fed raised its rate for the first time since 2023. It went up a little, to between 3.75% and 4.00%.
Why? Prices have been rising fast. Raising the rate makes borrowing cost more. People then spend less, and that helps stop prices going up so quickly.
The US president, Donald Trump, wanted rates to go down. The head of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, said the choice was serious and responsible.
The Fed said it might raise rates again before the end of the year. The next decision is on 28 October.
levels.why: Higher rates can slow rising prices, but they make loans cost more.

levels.headline: The central bank of the US puts up its interest rate
levels.body:
A central bank is a special bank that looks after the money for a whole country. The one in the United States is called the Federal Reserve. It chooses a number called the interest rate. Interest is the extra money you give back when you borrow money.
On 16 September the Fed made the number a little bigger. It had not done that since 2023. Now it is between 3.75% and 4.00%.
Why did it do that? Prices in the shops have been rising fast. When borrowing costs more, people spend less. Then prices stop going up so fast.
The US president did not like it. He wanted the number to go down. The head of the Fed said it was a serious and responsible choice.
The Fed might raise the number again before the end of the year.
levels.why: It is a way to try to stop prices from rising too fast.

levels.headline: A bank tries to slow down rising prices
levels.body:
Imagine everyone in your school wants the same toy. The shop sees this, and raises the price. That makes the toy cost more. Grown-ups call this prices going up.
Countries have a special bank that tries to stop prices rising too fast. In the United States it is called the Federal Reserve. One of the things it can do is make borrowing cost more. Borrowing is when you take money and promise to give it back later with a little extra.
This month, the Fed made the extra a little bigger. It had not done that for a few years. When borrowing costs more, people buy fewer things. Then prices stop going up so fast.
The Fed said it might do it again before the end of the year.
levels.why: It is a way to try to stop prices from rising too fast.
